newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE - Best-selling book awakens India poverty concerns.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Best-selling book awakens India poverty concerns.

text.p: A best-selling book that portrays life in India's poorest districts has reawakened hundreds of well-off Indians to the struggle millions of their countrymen endure each day just to survive.

As India prepares to celebrate its 50th year of independence from Britain, the stark prose of "Everybody Loves a Good Drought" by Bombay-based journalist P. Sainath is a sobering reminder that poverty is still the country's biggest problem.
"All of us Indians learn very early in life how to filter out poverty and other inconveniences," said David Davidar of Penguin India Ltd., the book's publisher.
"This book breaks through those filters."
Thirty-six percent of India's 950 million people scrabble for a living below the poverty line, the government estimates.
THE DARK SIDE OF ECONOMIC GROWTH
Sainath's book shines a harsh light on these deprived lives, say public policy and welfare experts.
The book shows how economic development has torn many of India's tribal groups out of their traditional ways of life and destroyed their forest environments.

The dam that is unfinished 20 years after work began, the village that was displaced three times over thirty years, and schoolrooms whose only occupants are village goats -- these are facets of their nation that few urban Indians see.
Madhu Dandavate, economist and chairman of India's Planning Commission, set the book virtually on par with a work of history by the country's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru.

"Like Nehru's 'Discovery of India', this book should have been called 'The Discovery of Poor India'," Dandavate, a former Indian finance minister, said. "If there is a second edition that is what it should be called."
FLYING OFF THE SHELVES
Bombay booksellers say the book sold out within a few days of arriving in the shops.
"It's selling exceedingly well," said Davidar. "The first edition of 2,000 copies has sold out. The next edition will be in the shops next week."

"We sold 250 copies in the first 10 days," said a salesman at Bombay's Strand Book Stall. At Crosswords, another popular bookshop, the book is sandwiched between best-selling tomes by New Age guru Deepak Chopra and software magnate Bill Gates.
It is rare for a non-fiction English title to do so well in India. If publishers can sell 3,000 copies of a fiction title they count themselves fortunate, book-sellers say.

The book, which has been prescribed as required reading for young civil servants, is soon to be adopted as a textbook for courses in journalism and development economics, and has its own website -- set up by an enthusiastic Canadian.
POOR'S RESILIENCE GIVES HOPE

"It does what no sterile debate on the Indian economy can do -- takes you right into the lives of the marginalised millions affected by it, whose hardship most of us cannot even begin to imagine," the Sunday Times of India newspaper said recently.
Sainath told Reuters that the ordinary Indians he met during his work on the book had demonstrated tremendous resilience and capabilities, which made him optimistic for India's future.
"If a man can drag 250 kg of coal loaded on a bicycle across 40 kms (25 miles) to earn 10 rupees ($0.28), then what is it that he cannot do if given a decent opportunity?" he asked.
"I don't know if it will spark an official debate, but I know it has made a very great impact on all those I meet who have read it," said publisher Davidar.
"I suspect we'll continue to sell a few hundred copies each year for several years to come."
